raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is a mechanical strategy to prevent thromboembolism in atrial fibrillation (AF), designed for patients in whom long-term oral anticoagulation is undesirable or unsafe. The rationale is anatomical and clinical: the left atrial appendage (LAA) is a trabeculated cul-de-sac with variable shape, contractility, and flow, and it is the dominant site of thrombus formation in non-valvular AF [1]. Surgical and pathological observations long suggested that appendage exclusion might reduce embolic risk [2], while epidemiological studies established AF as a major independent stroke risk factor [3]. Antithrombotic therapy remains foundational and highly effective [4], and direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) improved the risk-benefit profile of anticoagulation compared with warfarin [5-8]. Nevertheless, bleeding, frailty, falls, renal dysfunction, recurrent gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and patient preference create an important niche for non-pharmacological prevention.

Patient selection is central. LAAC is most often considered in patients with non-valvular AF, elevated CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, and a compelling reason to avoid indefinite anticoagulation. LAA morphology, size, depth, ostial ellipticity, and lobar anatomy influence feasibility and device choice, and certain morphologies have been associated with stroke risk [9]. Pre-procedural transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) or cardiac computed tomography is used to exclude LAA thrombus, define landing-zone dimensions, and plan transseptal puncture. Intraprocedural guidance is typically TEE or intracardiac echocardiography, with fluoroscopy.

The WATCHMAN device has the largest randomized evidence base. In PROTECT AF, LAAC was non-inferior to warfarin for a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death, but early procedural complications were more frequent than with medical therapy [10]. Longer follow-up showed durable protection and fewer hemorrhagic strokes [11]. PREVAIL, performed with more experienced operators and stricter criteria, did not meet all prespecified non-inferiority endpoints but showed improved procedural safety and low late event rates [12]. Patient-level and extended analyses suggested that, compared with warfarin, LAAC reduces hemorrhagic stroke, disabling/fatal stroke, cardiovascular or unexplained death, and non-procedural bleeding after the initial post-implant period [13,14].

Evidence in patients unsuitable for anticoagulation is less randomized but clinically influential. ASAP evaluated WATCHMAN in patients with contraindications to warfarin using antiplatelet-based therapy and reported stroke rates lower than expected for baseline risk [15]. Post-approval and European registry data confirmed high implant success with declining periprocedural complication rates, reflecting improvements in operator experience, imaging, and device iteration [16-18]. The next-generation WATCHMAN FLX improved conformability, sealing, recapturability, and safety; the PINNACLE FLX study reported high closure success and low serious adverse event rates [19].

The Amplatzer Cardiac Plug and Amulet devices offer a lobe-and-disc design that seals the ostium differently from the WATCHMAN plug concept. Early European experience demonstrated feasibility [20,21]. The Amulet IDE randomized trial compared Amulet with WATCHMAN and found non-inferiority for safety and effectiveness, with superior LAA sealing but more procedure-related complications in some analyses, emphasizing the trade-off between anatomy, device design, and operator familiarity [22]. Other approaches, including epicardial suture ligation, have been used selectively but have a smaller evidence base and distinct risks.

LAAC has also been compared with DOACs. PRAGUE-17 randomized high-risk AF patients to LAAC or DOAC therapy and found LAAC non-inferior for a composite of cardioembolic, bleeding, and cardiovascular outcomes [23]. Bleeding analyses across WATCHMAN trials suggest that once adjunctive antithrombotic therapy is discontinued, LAAC may reduce long-term non-procedural bleeding compared with warfarin [24]. These findings are important because the principal clinical value of LAAC is not simply replacing anticoagulation, but uncoupling long-term stroke prevention from continuous systemic anticoagulant exposure.

Complications remain clinically relevant. Pericardial effusion, device embolization, procedure-related stroke, vascular complications, and air embolism are uncommon but potentially serious. Device-related thrombus (DRT) occurs in a minority of patients and is associated with subsequent ischemic events; risk factors include prior stroke, permanent AF, large appendage, suboptimal implantation, and interruption or inadequacy of antithrombotic therapy [25]. Peridevice leak is common when very small, and its clinical significance varies by size and study; incomplete occlusion raised concern in PROTECT AF analyses [26]. Post-implant antithrombotic regimens have evolved from warfarin plus aspirin followed by dual antiplatelet therapy to DOAC- or antiplatelet-based strategies tailored to bleeding risk, although optimal regimens remain incompletely defined [27].

Contemporary national registry data show that LAAC has diffused into routine practice with high procedural success, but outcomes depend on patient selection, center experience, and standardized follow-up [28]. Surgical LAA occlusion during cardiac surgery reduces stroke in AF and supports the broader principle that eliminating the appendage can modify embolic risk [29]. TEE remains essential for identifying thrombus, guiding cardioversion and LAAC workflows, and detecting post-procedural DRT or leak [30]. Overall, percutaneous LAAC is best viewed as a complementary therapy to anticoagulation: not a universal substitute for DOACs, but an evidence-based option for carefully selected AF patients at high thromboembolic risk and unacceptable bleeding or anticoagulation burden.
